shortlist.raw_text: Recent advances in video generation call for reliable detection grounded in explicit forensic evidence. However, current methods primarily depend on single-pass chain-of-thought reasoning that overlooks brief or localized artifacts, or on predefined multi-agent workflows that offer limited flexibility in selecting relevant inspections. Even with adaptive investigation, optimizing the investigation policy alone does not directly improve the forensic capabilities of fixed experts. We introduce WeVisForensics, an agentic framework in which a main investigator agent coordinates a self-evolving library of forensic inspector sub-agents spanning visual and audio cues. The investigator learns which artifact type to examine, over which window, and when to conclude, and these interactions provide shared feedback for both levels of agents. Our dual-timescale policy optimization strategy, DTPO, closes this loop through fast reinforcement learning of the investigator and slower refinement of the inspectors, guided by annotated artifact intervals, to report subtle artifacts they once dismissed. Furthermore, we curate ForenCue-30K, combining role-specific forensic annotations and interaction trajectories to supervise individual inspections and their coordination, with an accompanying reinforcement-learning pool. Experiments show that WeVisForensics averages 95.2% detection accuracy across in-domain, out-of-domain and agentic benchmarks, 9.0% above the strongest prior detector, while grounding its verdicts in localized evidence.

shortlist.title: Mind2Act World: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action, and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation
shortlist.summary: Embodied intelligence aims to let robots perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback. shortlist.raw_text: Embodied intelligence aims to let robots perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback. Yet existing benchmarks either evaluate reasoning and execution within the same tasks or assess them separately without their composition, so they reveal little about whether a failure comes from reasoning, execution, or their composition. We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark of 30 simulated manipulation tasks from five real-world application domains. Each task has three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random), yielding 180 configurations. The tasks form three views: Mind tests decisions based on past observations, Act tests precise and timely execution, and Mind2Act combines both in closed-loop tasks where action outcomes guide later decisions. Comparing the three views shows whether a system lacks a capability or fails to compose capabilities it already has. A diagnosis harness further attributes the failed episodes of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition and summarizes each system in a profile card. Our evaluation of multimodal agents, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs) shows that competence in a single view does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. Even the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but in only 12.0% of Mind2Act episodes. The strongest agent retains task state but struggles with sustained contact, whereas end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state. These findings point to composing reasoning and execution through environmental feedback as the main open problem.

shortlist.raw_text: Video understanding, particularly with accompanying audio, remains a central challenge in multimodal intelligence. In this report, we introduce WeMM-Video, a family of Chinese-English bilingual omni-modal foundation models spanning 2B, 4B, 9B, and 35B-A3B variants. Centering on joint audio-visual perception and reasoning, WeMM-Video unifies text, image, audio, and video processing within a hybrid-thinking paradigm, seamlessly supporting both a non-thinking instruct mode for fast, direct responses and a thinking mode for explicit step-by-step reasoning. The models are trained on a large-scale multimodal corpus of approximately 1.2 trillion tokens through progressive pre-training and a multi-stage post-training pipeline incorporating multi-teacher OPD, anti-repetition MrDPO, and specialist RL. Evaluated across more than 120 benchmarks, WeMM-Video demonstrates superior performance in omni-modal video understanding and reasoning, while maintaining highly competitive capabilities across general audio, silent video, image, and text tasks. Specifically, in omni-modal video evaluations, our flagship WeMM-Video-35B-A3B establishes a new open-source state of the art, substantially outperforming proprietary models such as Qwen3.5-Omni-Flash and Seed2.0-Mini-0428 while narrowing the gap with the strong Gemini-3.0-Flash, and our compact WeMM-Video-9B surpasses the larger open-source Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct. We publicly release the WeMM-Video family along with our evaluation and reproduction pipeline to foster further research and development in the open-source community.

Title: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol get to the point faster but score lower on transparency than Claude

Text:
OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol give much shorter, more direct answers than their predecessors, but they are also less willing to admit uncertainty. Anthropic's Claude models score well ahead on transparency. The article GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol get to the point faster but score lower on transparency than Claude appeared first on The Decoder .

Article text (excerpt):
An Artificial Analysis evaluation shows how much OpenAI's communication style has changed. A comparison with Anthropic reveals sharp differences.
OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol give much shorter answers, get to the point faster, and impose less structure on their responses than their predecessors. At the same time, Artificial Analysis rates their tendency to admit uncertainty much lower.
Astra's average answer length dropped from 352 to 210 words, a 40 percent decrease. Sol went from 337 to 223 words, down 34 percent. Both models also use far fewer headings and em dashes. Astra's average number of headings per answer fell from 1.99 to 0.11, and Sol's from 1.85 to 0.25.
The Organization Index dropped sharply too. Astra went from 70 to 11, Sol from 86 to 27. This index combines four traits rated by AI judges, including answer structure, clarity, and Answer First, which measures whether a model immediately addresses the actual question. On that last trait, Astra jumped from 49 to 89 and Sol from 64 to 87. Scores for Natural Sounding language also climbed, from 58 to 100 for Astra and from 54 to 79 for Sol.
The biggest change shows up in the Admits Uncertainty trait. Astra's score fell from 96 to 24, and Sol's from 98 to 51. Unlike the raw word counts, these personality scores are relative rankings on a scale from 1 to 100. They show how strongly a given trait shows up in one model compared to all other tested models. A score of 24 doesn't mean Astra only admits uncertainty in 24 percent of its answers. Artificial Analysis published the evaluation on LinkedIn and X .
Our own comparison of all eight personality indexes shows clear gaps between OpenAI's latest models and Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5 . The indexes roll up 30 personality traits, each rated by AI judges based on model responses. All comparisons use the "max" model variants as listed by Artificial Analysis.
Anthropic's models score 81 and 90 on the Transparency Index, well above Astra (41) and Sol (57). This index covers five traits: Admits Uncertainty, Truthful, Disclaims Assumptions, Flags Nuances, and Sycophantic. That last one is scored inversely, since less flattery counts as a positive. Anthropic's models also lead on Organization.
Opus 5.5 stands out on the Informativeness Index with a score of 90, well ahead of the other three models. Its strongest individual traits include Information Dense and Evidence-Based reasoning.
The AA-PersonalityBench uses 900 English-language test questions that each model answers without a system prompt. A panel of three AI models evaluates anonymized answer pairs. For each comparison, one AI judge picks which answer shows the tested personality trait more strongly, or calls it a tie.
From these evaluations, Artificial Analysis calculates scores for 30 individual personality traits, which feed into eight higher-level indexes. The index values from 1 to 100 reflect each model's relative position among all tested models.
Separately, Artificial Analysis measures 21 communication traits that are counted directly rather than rated by AI judges. These include average answer length and the number of headings and em dashes per answer.
The personality scores describe differences in communication style, not overall answer quality. A lower Transparency Index doesn't necessarily mean a model gives wrong answers more often.
text:
OpenAI's newest model cut its average response length by 40 percent.

Its willingness to admit uncertainty dropped from 96 to 24 on the same test.

That trade-off changes how you should read its answers.

Artificial Analysis evaluated OpenAI's Astra and Sol against Anthropic's Claude models across 900 test questions.

They measured communication style using a panel of three AI judges, scoring models on a relative scale from 1 to 100.

OpenAI re-engineered how its models talk:
• Astra's average answer length fell from 352 to 210 words
• Its score for answering the question immediately jumped from 49 to 89
• Its score for natural sounding language reached 100
• Its score for admitting uncertainty dropped from 96 to 24

The model got faster and more direct.

It also stopped telling you when it is guessing.

Anthropic took a different path. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 90 on the Transparency Index, while Astra scored 41.

A lower transparency score does not mean a model makes more factual errors. It means it delivers uncertain answers with the exact same confidence as proven facts.

My read: concise answers feel better in the chat box, but hidden doubt is a dangerous trade-off for professional work.

Would you trade model honesty for conciseness?

Source: The Decoder
